title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 63-64
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 63 to 64 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'शुभाङ्गः शान्तिदः स्रष्टा कुमुदः कुवलेशयः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 63 to 64 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 63 to 64.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 63 to 64** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **शुभाङ्गः शान्तिदः स्रष्टा कुमुदः कुवलेशयः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**शुभाङ्गः शान्तिदः स्रष्टा कुमुदः कुवलेशयः । गोहितो गोपतिर्गोप्ता वृषभाक्षो वृषप्रियः ॥** **अनिवर्ती निवृत्तात्मा सङ्क्षेप्ता क्षेमकृच्छिवः । श्रीवत्सवक्षाः श्रीवासः श्रीपतिः श्रीमतां वरः ॥**

Fair of limb, the giver of peace, the creator is he. Soft as the water lily, resting upon the earth, is that God of gods. The well-wisher of cows, their lord and keeper, dear to dharma. He never turns back, rests in the Self and draws all into himself. The one who brings well-being, the auspicious one, is that God of gods. The mark of Shrivatsa on his chest, the home of Shri, her lord, and the best of the glorious.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 63 to 64 mean?
faq.a: Fair of limb, the giver of peace, the creator is he. Soft as the water lily, resting upon the earth, is that God of gods. The well-wisher of cows, their lord and keeper, dear to dharma. He never turns back, rests in the Self and draws all into himself. The one who brings well-being, the auspicious one, is that God of gods. The mark of Shrivatsa on his chest, the home of Shri, her lord, and the best of the glorious.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
